newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Unions, courts deliver fresh blows to Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Unions, courts deliver fresh blows to Milosevic.

text.p: Trade union support grew for protests against President Slobodan Milosevic in Serbia on Monday as a court handed the opposition a victory in a second town where elections were disputed.

Students, union members and supporters of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition began a fifth week of protests, protesting for the 29th straight day in Belgrade in a face-off with the government over its refusal to reinstate annulled local election results.
Zoran Djindjic, a prominent opposition leader, vowed at the Belgrade rally to organise a nationwide protest in the New Year to pile the pressure on Milosevic.

"One thousand people from each of 30 towns in Serbia will walk to join us here in Belgrade in the New Year, we will be world champions in protest marathons," he told the crowd, which was big but fell short of a record 250,000 people at the weekend.

The rallies have a carnival atmosphere despite expressing rock-solid opposition to Milosevic. Security forces have adopted a low profile although the memory of 1991 when Milosevic used tanks to crush street protests lingers.

In a second breakthrough for Zajedno, a court in the town of Smederevska Palanka ordered the local election commission to respect an annulled local election and give the municipal council to Zajedno. There was a similar order in Nis on Sunday.

There was more bad news for Milosevic when the traditionally pro-government Alliance of Independent Trade Unions of Yugoslavia, the nation's biggest and most influential union group, backed a smaller union's protests.

The alliance said it backed last week's decision by Nezavisnost to join anti-Milosevic protests which made it the first union to partipate in the rallies. Workers have cited grievances over pay and workers' conditions and rights.
Nezavisnost workers plan to demonstrate on Tuesday outside the Serbian parliament which is due to discuss several draft laws on labour and employment that workers believe will harm their interests.

The crisis has shaken Milosevic and gave the United States a fresh opportunity to fire a broadside at the weekend pressing him for democratic reform in Serbia in return for renewed access to capital on international finance markets.

Spain said former prime minister Felipe Gonzalez had been asked to lead an observer mission from the Organisation of Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) which Milosevic has invited to verify the elections.
"Regardless of the work of the OSCE mission, we shall not break off our protests for a second," defiant opposition leader Vuk Draskovic said.

In another example of international concern, a delegation from the Council of Europe Parliamentary Assembly on Monday visited Belgrade and spoke to officials. Its intention was to "get first-hand information on the crisis".

In Montenegro, which with Serbia makes up the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, parliament agreed to debate a draft opposition resolution supporting Serbia's opposition and condemning the Serbian authorities.
